analysis.one_liner: Forces dominant hub airlines to share underused gates and slots with smaller competitors to restore air travel competition.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill on a bipartisan basis, but it sat on the Senate calendar for more than a year and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted airline industry consolidation. The original version would have blocked mergers that gave one carrier more than 10% of national air traffic if the Transportation Secretary found they reduced competition, and would have required big hub airlines to prove that gates at airports they dominate would be shared fairly. By the time the committee reported it in December 2001, the merger restrictions were gone; what remained required the Transportation Secretary to investigate gate hoarding at the 35 busiest airports and to force major carriers to make underused gates, facilities, and landing slots available to rival carriers on fair terms.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, especially at hub airports where a single airline carries more than half of passengers and fares are documented to be higher. The bill's own findings cite Transportation Department data that fares are relatively higher at such dominated hubs and that low-fare competitors save passengers $6.3 billion a year. Smaller and low-fare airlines also benefit, since they could compete for gates and slots that dominant carriers hold but underuse.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Secretary to investigate how major airlines assign and use gates, facilities, and slots at the 35 busiest US airports, and to force major carriers to make underused assets available to rivals on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory terms if competition would be enhanced [S3][S4].
Makes it an unfair method of competition for a dominant airline at a dominated hub airport to let gates and facilities sit unused while refusing requests from other carriers to use them [S3][S4].

Overturns the effect of 'majority-in-interest clauses' that let a dominant airline block an airport authority from building new gates for competitors, by directing the Secretary to ensure gates are available on fair terms at such airports [S3][S4].

Authorizes $300 million in airport improvement grants from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund for gates and facilities that increase competition, with priority for projects serving small and mid-sized communities [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant hub airlines, which would have to give up exclusive control of underused gates, facilities, and landing slots to rival carriers, and which under the original bill would have faced a new merger review and a cap blocking acquisitions that gave a carrier more than 10% of national passenger traffic. Passengers could see some operational disruption if gate reassignments complicate hub scheduling.

drawbacks.text: The original version would have given the Transportation Secretary power to block airline mergers that the Justice Department might allow, adding a second federal review of up to 180 days for the same deal, which carriers and merger experts could reasonably call duplicative [S4].

The version the committee reported dropped the merger-review provisions entirely, so it addressed gate access but left untouched the industry consolidation the bill's own findings warned would push the five largest airlines toward about 83% of the market [S3][S4].

Forced sharing of gates and landing slots at congested hub airports could impose scheduling and efficiency costs on airlines that invested in those facilities, a tradeoff the bill acknowledges by directing the Secretary to weigh whether reassignment improves competition 'without compromising safety or creating scheduling, efficiency, or other problems' [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For travelers the benefits are concrete: gate hoarding and majority-in-interest clauses are direct barriers to low-fare competition at hub airports, where fares are documented to be higher. The original merger cap was a stronger but blunter tool that duplicated Justice Department antitrust review, and the committee stripped it. The reported gate-access provisions were narrower, more incremental, and low-risk for travelers; their main cost falls on dominant airlines' operational control of hub facilities.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably and it was placed on the Senate calendar on December 19, 2001, but it never came up for a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 28, 2001 by Senator Hollings with five cosponsors, three Democrats and two Republicans, amid a wave of proposed airline mergers including United-US Airways and American-TWA [S4][S5][S6].
The Commerce Committee held hearings on March 13, 2001 and ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on March 15 [S6].

The committee reported the bill on December 19, 2001 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute that removed the original merger-review and merger-cap provisions, leaving the gate- and facility-access provisions [S3][S4][S6].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 300 on December 19, 2001, and no floor vote was ever taken before the Congress ended [S1][S6].

The bill's findings cited Transportation Department and GAO studies showing higher fares and weaker competition at hub airports where one airline carries more than half of passengers, and estimated low-fare competitors save passengers $6.3 billion annually [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant hub airlines came out ahead: because the bill never became law, they kept exclusive control of underused gates and slots at the airports they dominate, and no new merger review or gate-sharing requirement was ever imposed. Air travelers at those hubs gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was split evenly between the parties (3 of 49 Democrats and 2 of 49 Republicans) and the committee reported it favorably; no party-line vote was ever recorded because the Senate never voted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required dominant carriers to share underused gates, facilities, and slots with rivals at the 35 busiest airports, and the original version would have capped mergers creating carriers with more than 10% of national traffic. Because it died, these carriers kept exclusive hub assets and unrestricted merger freedom.

The bill would have given them access to scarce gates and slots at dominated hub airports on fair terms, letting them compete where they are currently locked out. Their entry is associated with substantially lower fares for travelers.

The bill authorized $300 million in grants for competitive-access gates and facilities and would have freed airport authorities from majority-in-interest clauses that a dominant airline can use to block new gate construction.
